scenario: AITA - For not extending a specific invitation to two nieces for an annual family event that everyone is invited to? | Every year, on the last day of March, we gather as a family to celebrate my father-in-law’s life at a specific restaurant. He passed away many years ago, and that was his favorite place to eat. My mother-in-law foots the bill as part of the celebration and everyone in the family that can attend is always welcome. Sometimes people bring friends and it is never a big deal and we all celebrate a great man. This year, we had 3 of the 4 of my mother-in-law’s kids and their families come and had a wonderful time. My wife took a picture and posted it to social media to honor her dad. The unrepresented kid (I say kid loosely as she is over 50) took exception to this and flew off the handle because their family didn’t get an invitation and were purposely excluded. It is an open invitation, and she and all her children are adults with working phones. AITA for not reaching out to them and explicitly inviting them? Or should they know they are welcome (since they have been every other year) and take the initiative to just come? I didn’t get an invite and I showed up, so maybe IATA for a different reason.

First, the event is an annual family gathering to celebrate the father-in-law's life. It happens every year on the last day of March at a specific restaurant. The mother-in-law pays for it, and everyone in the family who can attend is welcome. Sometimes people bring friends, and it's not a big deal. They all celebrate this great man.

This year, three out of four of the mother-in-law's kids and their families attended. They had a wonderful time, and the wife took a picture and posted it on social media to honor her dad. The unrepresented kid (who is actually over 50) got upset because her family wasn't invited and felt purposely excluded. She claims they were excluded even though it's an open invitation, and she and her children have working phones.

The question is whether the person is AITA for not reaching out to them and explicitly inviting them. Or should they know they're welcome since they've been attending every other year and take the initiative to come? The person mentions that they didn't get an invite but showed up, so maybe they're AITA for a different reason.

Hmm, so the key points here are:

1. The event is open to everyone in the family, with an open invitation.
2. The unrepresented niece felt excluded because she wasn't explicitly invited.
3. The family has been attending every other year, so they should know they're welcome.
4. The person didn't send an explicit invitation but assumed they knew about it.

I think the main issue here is the expectation of the invitation. If it's an open invitation, does everyone assume they're welcome without needing a specific invite? Or is it the responsibility of the organizers to send out explicit invitations to each family member?

In this case, the mother-in-law is footing the bill, so she's the one organizing. The person didn't send an explicit invitation, but the niece felt excluded. The niece is over 50, so she's an adult, and her children are also adults with working phones. So, they should be able to communicate and find out about the event.

But the niece felt that she and her family were purposely excluded. That's a strong emotion, and it's important to consider why she felt that way. Maybe she felt left out because she wasn't personally invited, even though the event is open to everyone.

On the other hand, the person didn't send an explicit invitation because they assumed she knew about it, especially since she's been attending every other year. So, maybe the person isn't at fault because they didn't exclude her; they just didn't send a specific invite.

But in terms of moral acceptability, is it wrong to not send an explicit invitation when someone feels excluded? Or is it acceptable because the invitation was open?

I think the key here is communication. If the event is open, but someone feels excluded because they weren't personally invited, that's a problem. The organizers should make sure that everyone feels included, even if it's an open invitation.

So, in this case, the person didn't send an explicit invitation, which led to the niece feeling excluded. Therefore, the action of not sending an explicit invitation might be considered morally unacceptable because it caused someone to feel excluded, even if the intention wasn't to exclude.

Alternatively, maybe the niece is overreacting because she should know about the event since it's annual and she's been attending. But feelings of exclusion are valid, and it's better to err on the side of making everyone feel included.

So, considering all this, I think the action of not extending a specific invitation might be morally unacceptable because it led to someone feeling excluded, even if the intention wasn't to exclude.
